{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2023}}
{{Use British English|date=August 2012}}
'''Peter Sykes''', [[Royal Society of Chemistry|FRSC]] (19 February 1923 – 24 October 2003<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/comment/obituaries/article999377.ece |title=Archived copy |access-date=20 April 2011 |archive-date=3 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121103122155/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/comment/obituaries/article999377.ece |url-status=dead }}</ref>) was a British [[chemist]] and a former fellow<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.admin.cam.ac.uk/reporter/2003-04/special/03/1.html |title=Reporter 2/10/03: CHRIST'S COLLEGE |publisher=Admin.cam.ac.uk |date=2 October 2003 |accessdate=2011-11-20}}</ref> and vice-master of [[Christ's College, Cambridge|Christ's College]], [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]].

He is the author of the [[Undergraduate education|undergraduate]]-level [[organic chemistry]] [[textbook]] ''A Guidebook to Mechanism in Organic Chemistry''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pearsonhighered.com/educator/academic/product/0,3110,0582446953,00.html |title=Pearson – Guidebook to Mechanism in Organic Chemistry, 6/E – Peter Sykes |publisher=Pearsonhighered.com |accessdate=2011-11-20}}</ref> A textbook on [[Mechanism (philosophy)|mechanistic]] organic chemistry, it is used all over the world for different competitive examinations.{{Citation needed|date=January 2021}}

He was born in [[Chorlton]], the younger son of John George Sykes and Alice (née Booth). He attended [[Rydal Penrhos|Rydal School]].

Peter Sykes married Joyce Tyler in 1946. They had three children: Nicholas Peter (1949), Stephen (1951) and Helen (1956). He died at 33 Cavendish Avenue, Cambridge.
